claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained loading is governed primarily by interface-mediated dislocation activity.
Compositional complexity and short-range order modulate interface-mediated dislocation activity.
FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers to dislocations.
FCC/BCC interfaces act as sources of dislocations.
Severe lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Local chemical fluctuations impede dislocation motion.
Creep is dominated by interface-controlled mechanisms rather than bulk diffusion or conventional dislocation glide.
The proposed initial coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with well-defined interfaces.
The coating will be subjected to constant stress or load at elevated temperature.
The tested temperature and stress should permit measurable creep while remaining below conditions causing delamination or melting.
Compositional complexity and short-range order suppress bulk diffusion.
Compositional complexity and short-range order suppress conventional dislocation glide.
High-entropy-alloy multilayers will have a lower steady-state creep rate than conventional compositionally simpler multilayers.
High-entropy-alloy multilayers will show a more pronounced transition to interface-controlled deformation than conventional metallic multilayers.
Dislocations will pile up at or be absorbed by FCC/BCC interfaces.
Bulk dislocation activity will be limited in the high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
Conventional Cu/Nb or Ni/Al multilayers under similar loading and temperature conditions exhibit creep dominated by bulk dislocation glide or diffusion.
The hypothesis applies only while the nanoscale layers, interface integrity, and compositional complexity are retained.
The hypothesis does not apply after layer coarsening, interface degradation, or compositional homogenization.
Direct experimental evidence for creep mechanisms in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is lacking, leaving the magnitude of creep suppression and the role of short-range order uncertain.
